blocks.text: Verses 9–10 warn against the desire to be rich and identify love of money—not money itself—as a root of many kinds of evil. The chapter does not end by rejecting wealthy people as such: verses 17–19 tell those who are rich not to place their hope in unstable wealth, but to do good and share generously.

The opening addresses enslaved people and instructs them how to act toward their masters, including masters who share their faith. It regulates conduct within slavery; it does not abolish the ownership of one person by another. The closing warning likewise identifies “knowledge falsely so called” as a polemical label, but its precise target is unknown and should not automatically be equated with a later movement, with science, or with education.

The instructions to enslaved people should not be transferred directly to modern employment in order to justify worker exploitation, abusive supervision, union suppression, or forced labor. The text addresses a coercive arrangement rather than presenting that arrangement as an ideal.

The call to contentment challenges profiteering and acquisitive desire, but it should not be used to shame poverty, oppose fair wages, or counsel people to accept deprivation. In the same chapter, the rich are warned against arrogance and misplaced trust and are directed toward generosity.
